reading.body:
Construction AI is measured, not guessed: Census BTOS surveys firms fortnightly, AGC tracks contractor adoption, and BuiltWorlds plus proptech trackers follow the tools, with computer-vision safety monitoring, BIM clash detection, and autonomous site scanning as the working deployments.

The pattern is narrow and physical. The named deployments all watch the jobsite or check a digital model against reality before concrete is poured, so the value is in catching discrepancies early, not in generating designs or schedules. That makes construction AI an on-site perception and verification problem, where the binding constraints are accurate site data and timely action before work proceeds.

What the data does not show is how widely these tools are used, what they save, or how often they fail. It establishes that adoption is tracked through a federal survey, a trade body, a research network, and venture flow, but those sources still reflect firms and startups that choose to report, not the entire industry.

summary: Computer-vision safety monitoring, BIM clash detection, and autonomous site scanning are the working deployments - the sector's AI mostly watches the jobsite and checks the model against reality before concrete is poured.

analysis.body:
The most solid number available for construction AI use comes from the Census Bureau's Business Trends and Outlook Survey, which asks firms directly whether they used AI in the last two weeks. For Construction (NAICS 23), the latest reading is 17.2%, up from 15.4% in the prior period. That is a measured adoption rate rather than an estimate, and it is the figure a reader should anchor on when comparing construction with other sectors.

What firms are doing with the technology is described mainly through the industry's research and conference networks rather than through survey breakdowns. BuiltWorlds, which runs sector intelligence for buildings and infrastructure, frames its programming around data centers and AI infrastructure at its Buildings Conference and devotes a separate annual AI/ML Conference to artificial intelligence and machine learning in the AEC/O industry. That event covers existing and emerging solutions and use cases across the construction, building, and operation process, strategies for implementation at the project and enterprise levels, and case studies of how companies are using specific solutions and what they learned. The curated coverage on this page points to computer-vision safety monitoring, BIM clash detection, and autonomous site scanning as the concrete applications in view.

The money and vendor activity cluster around events and networks that span construction and real estate. CREtech describes its New York gathering as a real estate AI conference bringing together 3,000 leaders, 150 speakers, and 20,000+ 1:1 meetings, with owners, developers, investors, occupiers, construction companies, brokers, and technology leaders attending, and it says every session is led by operators actively deploying AI across their portfolios. The curated points note that CREtech and MetaProp track venture flow across architecture, engineering, and construction technology alongside property tech, which places contech within the broader proptech capital pool rather than treating it separately.

On the trade body side, the Associated General Contractors of America represents over 27,000 member firms and, per the curated points, surveys technology adoption and safety-technology compliance across US builders, making its data the adoption record for the trade. The AGC page itself emphasizes safety programming, including a San Diego event for construction safety professionals, which aligns with the safety-monitoring use case rather than with general adoption statistics.

ROI evidence in this material is thin. The sources describe case studies and lessons learned through BuiltWorlds programming and operator-led sessions at CREtech, but the excerpts do not report specific returns, cost savings, or payback figures for construction deployments. A reader looking for quantified ROI will not find it here.

On risk and regulation, the sources are largely silent. Nothing in the excerpts addresses permitting, liability, jobsite safety regulation of AI systems, or data governance. The nearest signal is AGC's emphasis on safety-technology compliance, which suggests that safety-related technology adoption is tracked against compliance expectations, but the material does not go further.

For a contractor deciding whether to deploy, the takeaway is modest and grounded. Adoption is real and rising, at 17.2% of firms per the Census Bureau, which means most firms still have not adopted. The visible use cases are safety monitoring, clash detection, and site scanning, and the industry's knowledge infrastructure, through BuiltWorlds, AGC, and the CREtech and MetaProp tracking of venture flow, is organized enough to learn from peers before committing. The sources do not supply ROI benchmarks or regulatory guidance, so those questions need to be answered elsewhere.

https://cretech.com/.brief: According to the page, CREtech New York 2026 will be held at the Javits Center in New York City on October 20, 21, 2026, and will bring together 3,000 leaders, 150 speakers, and more than 20,000 pre-scheduled 1:1 meetings. The event is described as a leading real-estate AI conference where sessions are led by operators actively deploying AI in their portfolios, offering real strategy rather than theory. The conference aims to connect owners, developers, investors, occupiers, construction firms, brokers, and tech leaders to discuss AI’s impact on real-estate assets. Tickets are limited, and sponsors and partners are said to represent companies shaping the future of real-estate in the age of AI.

https://www.agc.org/.brief: The Associated General Contractors of America describes itself as serving more than 27,000 member firms, offering a range of services intended to address members' needs and concerns. According to the organisation, those services aim to improve the quality of construction and to protect the public interest. The page also promotes an event in San Diego that it says brings together construction safety professionals from around the country to share ideas, build relationships, and take proven solutions back to their teams.

https://builtworlds.com/.brief: BuiltWorlds operates a membership network for buildings and infrastructure professionals. The organization hosts an annual Buildings Conference addressing innovation in building development, design, materials and systems, with particular focus on data centers and AI infrastructure. It also runs an annual AI/ML Conference exploring artificial intelligence and machine learning adoption across the architecture, engineering, construction and operations industry, covering implementation strategies, use cases, and lessons learned from companies deploying these technologies.
